notes.meaning: The bridegroom announces that he has entered his garden to gather his spices and feast on sweet treats. In the traditional view, Christ gladly accepts the welcome of his church and takes delight in the obedience and spiritual fruit of his people. He then calls his companions to feast abundantly on the rich gifts of his grace.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many scholars view this verse as celebrating the consummation of married love on the wedding night, with the surrounding chorus or guests rejoicing in their union.

notes.meaning: The bride rests in bed while her thoughts stay fixed on her beloved, who knocks and begs her to let him in out of the damp night air. In the traditional reading, this shows a believer growing spiritually lazy even though true faith still lives in the heart. Christ calls patiently and tenderly, bearing hardships to wake his sleeping people.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars read this scene as an anxious dream that reveals the woman's inner hesitation and longing rather than an actual event.

notes.meaning: The woman makes flimsy excuses about having already taken off her clothes and washed her feet for bed. Allegorically, this exposes how easily Christians make silly excuses when Christ calls them to duty or fellowship. Sloth makes people unwilling to bear even small inconveniences for the Lord.

The lover reaches through the door opening to unlatch the bolt, and the woman's heart stirs with deep affection for him. In the spiritual sense, when gentle words fail to rouse the soul, the Holy Spirit works directly on the conscience. This inner touch melts stubbornness and awakens fresh love for Christ.

The bride finally rises to let her beloved in, and her hands are covered with sweet-smelling perfume left on the bolt. Traditionally, this shows that Christ leaves behind the sweet influence of his grace even when he seems to step back. When a believer begins to obey, duty becomes much sweeter than expected.

When she opens the door, her beloved has already walked away, leaving her crushed and desperate. In the traditional reading, Christ sometimes withdraws his comforting presence to correct his people for their careless delays. Even in her distress, she still claims him as her beloved and seeks him through earnest prayer.

The city watchmen find the woman wandering the streets at night, beat her, and strip away her light outer cloak. Allegorically, this represents harsh or unfaithful church leaders who misjudge an aching believer and wound tender consciences. Those seeking Christ often face unfair rebukes from the very people who should care for them.

The wounded bride begs the daughters of Jerusalem to tell her beloved that she is faint from longing for him. In the life of faith, this pictures an awakened believer asking fellow Christians for prayer and spiritual help. Gracious souls hurt more from feeling distant from Christ than from any worldly trouble.

The women of the city ask why her beloved is so much better than any other man that she pleads so desperately. Traditionally, seeing a Christian's deep love for Jesus stirs up curiosity in those who do not yet know him well. Their question gives the believer an opportunity to describe the surpassing glory of Christ.

The bride declares that her beloved has a bright, healthy complexion and stands out above ten thousand men. In the traditional picture, his dazzling whiteness points to his spotless holiness, while his ruddy color points to his suffering and shed blood. He stands supreme above every other ruler or savior.

She describes his head as pure, fine gold and his wavy locks of hair as black as a raven. Allegorically, the gold represents Christ's divine majesty and supreme authority over all creation. His full, dark hair represents his unchanging vigor, strength, and youth.

She compares his eyes to doves resting by clear streams, washed clean and set like gems. Traditionally, this speaks of Christ's pure, gentle, and loving watchfulness over his people. His eyes look on his friends with deep tenderness and perfect truth.

The beloved's cheeks look like fragrant garden terraces, and his lips drop precious, sweet-smelling oil. Allegorically, this pictures the joyful comfort believers experience in the presence of Christ. His words and promises bring life and spiritual fragrance to all who listen.

The bride pictures his hands as rods of gold set with jewels and his body as polished ivory adorned with blue stones. In the spiritual view, this shows that all of Christ's works are rich, pure, and effective. His deep, inward compassion toward his people is firm, noble, and beautiful.

She describes his legs as stately marble pillars on golden bases, and his overall presence as grand as the cedars of Mount Lebanon. Traditionally, this highlights the firmness, stability, and enduring strength of Christ's ways. He is fully able to uphold his people and bear the weight of his eternal kingdom.

The bride concludes by saying his words are pure sweetness and everything about him is delightful. Allegorically, believers find that Christ is completely lovely in his person, his teachings, and his grace. He is not only their Lord and King, but also their personal, faithful friend.
